title: Churchill and the Art of Persuasion
author: Anya Leonard
summary: Anya Leonard reads Churchill's June 4, 1940 'We Shall Fight on the Beaches' speech through the classical rhetorical tradition of Aristotle and Cicero. She shows that Churchill first builds ethos by telling Parliament the hard truth about Dunkirk, then supplies logos through the detailed account of the battle, and only afterward unleashes pathos in the famous peroration. She credits Cicero's De Oratore for the principle that emotional climax must be built and earned, and points to anaphora and the widening geographic sweep of 'we shall fight' as devices that accumulate emotion. She then asks whether Churchill knew any of this, noting his Harrow training in memorization and declamation and his youthful essay The Scaffolding of Rhetoric, in which he concludes oratory is neither wholly bestowed nor wholly acquired but cultivated.
points: Churchill earns credibility by refusing to dress up Dunkirk as a victory, which fits Aristotle's view that ethos is established through the speech itself.
The long factual middle of the speech is the logos on which the emotional crescendo rests, so the famous lines land because they were earned.
Cicero's warning against opening with the most stirring lines explains why Churchill makes his audience wait for the peroration.
Anaphora and the inward movement from France to British streets accumulate emotion before the pattern breaks on 'We shall never surrender.'
Churchill's own conclusion that rhetorical power is cultivated rather than simply innate or taught shows the classical tradition working through a non-classical education.
quotes: Of all the talents bestowed upon men, none is so precious as the gift of oratory. He who enjoys it wields a power more durable than that of a great king. He is an independent force in the world.

Importantly, he does not hide from the precarious situation of the Allies nor the difficult implications of what occurred at Dunkirk. Indeed, Churchill goes out of his way to prevent any premature sense of triumph, reminding Parliament that, “We must be very careful not to assign to this deliverance the attributes of a victory. Wars are not won by evacuations.

In his book Rhetoric, the fourth-century BC philosopher outlined three fundamental modes of persuasion: ethos, pathos, and logos. These are the character and credibility of the speaker, the emotions of the audience, and the argument itself.
Churchill does not tell Parliament they should believe him, he presents his trustworthiness instead by not concealing anything or trying to diminish the hardships they are facing.

Cicero, the famed statesman and speaker, wrote extensively about the construction of a speech in his De Oratore, completed in 55 BC. He even warns against leaping immediately into the passionate portion of an address.
There is also an interesting rhetorical device at work here: anaphora. This is the purposeful repetition of the same words at the beginning of successive phrases.

Churchill also wonders how much of great oratory can actually be taught. Rhetorical power, he concludes, is “neither wholly bestowed nor wholly acquired, but cultivated”... an interesting conclusion considering his own unconventional education.
